analysis.one_liner: Charges hardrock miners a small royalty and yearly fees on federal land, with the money going to abandoned-mine cleanup.
analysis.headline: A bill to charge a 2% royalty on hardrock mining from federal land and fund abandoned-mine cleanup was introduced with 4 Republican sponsors and died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under an 1872 law, hardrock mining companies can take gold, silver, copper, uranium, and other minerals from federal land without paying the government any royalty. This bill would have changed that modestly: a 2% royalty on the net proceeds from minerals produced on federal land, plus small claim-staking and yearly fees, with the money going into a new fund to seal old mine shafts and clean up abandoned mines that pollute water and endanger communities. It would also have given mining claim holders permanent rights to use federal land in exchange for the fees, created a new federal office to inventory the nation's mineral resources, and convened a national summit aimed at greatly expanding domestic uranium production. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, two groups would have gained. Mining companies would have gained certainty: the bill let them pay a 2% royalty on net proceeds — a small amount after generous deductions — plus modest fees, in exchange for guaranteed, permanent rights to use and occupy federal land for mining, and it pushed for greatly expanded access to uranium reserves. Communities living near abandoned hardrock mines would have gained a dedicated cleanup fund paying for sealing mine openings, treating polluted mine drainage, and reclaiming scarred land, with public health and safety projects prioritized.

how_it_helps.text: It creates an Abandoned Locatable Mine Reclamation Fund and a grant program, run through the Office of Surface Mining, for sealing old mine entries, treating acid mine drainage, and reclaiming abandoned hardrock mine land and water — with priority given to protecting public health and safety.

It imposes, for the first time under the general mining laws, a 2% royalty on net proceeds of locatable minerals produced from federal land, plus a $35 location fee, a $25 annual abandoned-mine fee, and a $125 annual maintenance fee per claim.
It gives mining claim holders 'security of tenure': paying the fees secures their right to use and occupy federal land for all mineral activities, from claim location through mine closure.

It establishes a new Office of Economic Geology at the USGS, a recurring national mineral resource inventory, and a national uranium summit charged with recommending how to expand domestic uranium production to 30% of U.S. demand by 2030.

analysis.who_pays: The public would have paid in foregone revenue: under the 1872 Mining Law, minerals worth billions belong to the government, and this bill would have set the public's return at 2% of net proceeds — with deductions that could shrink it further — a rate far below what oil, gas, and coal companies pay for federal minerals. The bill also would have locked in mining companies' long-term rights to use federal land, and pushed open more uranium-bearing land to development, with the environmental risks borne by nearby communities.

drawbacks.text: The 2% royalty is on 'net proceeds' — gross sales minus a long list of deductions including extraction, processing, transport, marketing, insurance, depreciation, state and local taxes, and even other royalties paid — so the effective payment to the public would be far below 2% of the value of the minerals, and the Secretary could further waive, suspend, or reduce the royalty on any claim to 'promote development.'

Operators with annual net proceeds under $100,000 pay no royalty at all, and the fee waivers for anyone holding up to 50 claims (including affiliates and subsidiaries) mean many claim holders could keep paying almost nothing while securing perpetual rights to use federal land.

The bill codifies 'security of tenure' — payment of a $125 annual fee secures a claim holder's right to use and occupy federal lands before and after a mineral discovery — entrenching the mining industry's long-term access to public land while directing only abandoned-mine fees automatically to cleanup, with the rest of the fund subject to yearly appropriations.

The uranium section sets a policy goal of producing 30% of the nation's uranium domestically by 2030 and frames expanded access to reserves such as the Arizona Strip — near the Grand Canyon region — as a national security priority, pushing development of public lands without new environmental conditions beyond existing standards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's real benefits — a dedicated stream of money for cleaning up abandoned hardrock mines that pollute streams and endanger communities — were real but modest, because the money came from tiny fees and a royalty that was small by design: 2% of net proceeds, not of gross value, with deductions that could erase most of the difference, an exemption for operators under $100,000 in annual net proceeds, and discretionary authority for the Secretary to waive or suspend the royalty entirely. Meanwhile the bill would have permanently locked in mining companies' broad rights to use and occupy federal land. An honest supporter would acknowledge that this was reform written to cost the industry as little as possible; an honest critic would acknowledge that any royalty and any dedicated cleanup fund was more than the 1872 law provided.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Natural Resources Committee, which passed it down to a subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended — no hearing vote, no floor vote, nothing.

narrative.text: Rep. Doug Lamborn introduced the bill on July 14, 2009, 'for himself and Mr. Bishop of Utah' — the only original cosponsors — stating its purpose as 'a fair return to the public, security of tenure to holders of mining claims and mill sites, and cleanup of abandoned mine lands.'
The House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources the same day, and on July 17, 2009 referred it to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources.
No further action was ever taken: the bill sat in subcommittee for the rest of the 111th Congress, which ended January 3, 2011, without a hearing, a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
Three other House Republicans signed on as cosponsors; no House Democrat did.

The bill would have charged mining companies a 2% royalty on net proceeds from minerals produced on federal land, $35 to stake a claim, and $125 a year to keep each claim, with the abandoned-mine fees and excess royalties deposited into a new cleanup fund for grants to states and tribes.

The royalty was set on 'net proceeds' — allowing deductions for extraction, processing, transport, marketing, insurance, depreciation, state taxes, and more — and was waived entirely for operations with less than $100,000 in annual net proceeds.

The bill also included a 'National Uranium Summit Act' directing the Interior Secretary to convene a summit with uranium industry representatives and report policies to expand domestic uranium production, targeting 30% of U.S. demand by 2030.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies came out ahead: the bill died before it could impose even the modest 2% royalty, so they continue to extract gold, silver, copper, and other hardrock minerals from federal land without paying any royalty under the 1872 Mining Law, while taxpayers and communities near abandoned mines get no new cleanup fund.

for.name: Rob Bishop of Utah
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Nick Rahall
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled it for a hearing or markup; the bill went no further than a subcommittee referral.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and no House Democrat signed on; the bill died in the subcommittee of the Democrat-controlled Natural Resources Committee without any vote.

industries.note: Because the bill died, mining companies continue to take gold, silver, copper, and other hardrock minerals from federal land with no royalty at all under the 1872 law. The bill itself would have entrenched their position in a different way: a low 2% royalty on net proceeds (far below what federal law charges oil and gas producers, which pay royalties on gross value) plus codified 'security of tenure' — permanent rights to use and occupy public land in exchange for a $125 annual fee.

industries.industry: Uranium mining and nuclear fuel industry
industries.note: The bill's 'National Uranium Summit Act' would convene industry representatives to chart a policy of expanding domestic uranium production to 30% of national demand by 2030, with findings highlighting the Arizona Strip near the Grand Canyon as the nation's highest-grade uranium region. The industry's gain in access to public lands would come at the expense of land protection and the public's royalty return.

Claim holders with 50 or fewer claims would have maintenance and abandoned-mine fees waived or sharply reduced, so small operators could keep claims cheaply — though the definition includes affiliates and parent companies, allowing larger operations to qualify through subsidiaries.

industries.industry: States and tribes with abandoned hardrock mines
industries.note: States and Indian tribes would receive federal grants to seal mine openings, treat polluted drainage, and reclaim abandoned mine land, prioritizing public health and safety. Because the bill died, no such dedicated funding stream was created.
